title: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it will still be clear that the smallest known bodies which are described as organisms draw nigh towards molecular magnitudes, and we must recognise that the subdivision of the organism cannot proceed to an indefinite extent, and in all probability cannot go very much further than it appears to have done in these already discovered forms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Lower limit of size”. Scope: the smallest micro-organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern cell-size and genome data can directly evaluate whether known organisms approach a plausible molecular lower bound and whether much smaller forms have been found. The phrase cannot be much smaller remains imprecise, and completeness of discovery cannot be guaranteed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compile verified dimensions, genome sizes and molecular inventories of the smallest free-living and host-dependent organisms, estimate the minimum components required for autonomous life, and compare discovered cells with that bound. Organisms substantially below the proposed scale would refute the historical prediction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Reported ultramicrobe sizes can reflect filtration artifacts or nonliving particles.

Dependence on hosts blurs the definition of organism and minimum autonomous machinery.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.65
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.65
operationalizability: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Cell dimensions and the sizes of the molecular parts that fill them are both in public databases, so the 1917 comparison of a minute micrococcus with molecular magnitudes can be rerun directly. The further claim that organisms cannot be much smaller is only partly closed by catalogs of known cells, and the organism boundary matters. The data can confirm that the known minimum is near a packing limit, without exhausting undiscovered smaller forms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare the lower tail of free-living cell diameter with the volume of a minimal genome plus ribosomes. The claim is supported if that tail sits near the packing floor corresponding to tens of thousands of proteins; it is weakened if diverse free-living organisms are far smaller than that floor allows.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Where an object stops being an organism and becomes a virus is a definitional boundary at the lower limit.

Culture collections miss many of the smallest uncultured cells.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.6
analysis feasibility: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.55
data existence: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.75
